title: A fresh look at Australian stick insects reveals overlooked species
summary:
Discovering a species does not always mean finding an animal nobody has seen before. Sometimes the animal has been photographed, collected and studied for years, but scientists have placed it in the wrong group. A new study of Australian stick insects shows how that can happen.

Researchers at the University of Sydney reexamined Australian members of Anchiale, a genus, or group of closely related species. Insects previously classified as just two species actually represent five. Together, they occur from northern New South Wales along coastal Queensland and into tropical northern Australia.

The team identified two previously unrecognized species and restored recognition of a third that had gone unrecognized for decades. The findings were published in Austral Entomology.

One particularly surprising case involved a large insect already familiar to scientists and insect enthusiasts. Evidence showed that it had been incorrectly identified for decades. It is now recognized as a separate species, Anchiale robusta.

To untangle these identities, the researchers combined DNA analysis with museum specimens, field surveys, citizen science observations and studies of insects raised in captivity. DNA provides inherited biological information, while specimens and observations let researchers compare the animals themselves. Using several kinds of evidence helped them examine distinctions that earlier classifications had missed.

There was already plenty of information to work with. More than 1,000 citizen science observations had been submitted through iNaturalist and the Atlas of Living Australia. Yet the study found overlooked diversity among insects that had also received decades of scientific attention.

Another newly described species, Anchiale mabiensis, comes from the critically endangered Mabi rainforest on Queensland’s Atherton Tablelands. Its eggs have a distinctive structural lid. The researchers say this feature had not previously been documented in any stick insect or its closest relatives.

The revised classification could also help forestry and agriculture. One stick insect known for occasional large population outbreaks, during which insects strip leaves from trees, turned out to represent more than one species. Distinguishing those species could help researchers and land managers better understand and manage future impacts.

The team also identified a possible additional species from Cape York. Its identity remains unconfirmed because more specimens are needed.

Lead author Dr. Braxton Jones described taxonomy, the science of identifying and classifying organisms, as detective work. He said the findings show how much scientists still have to learn about insect diversity. He also emphasized protecting threatened ecosystems and documenting species before they disappear without being recognized.
why_it_matters: The study shows that even well-studied insects can include overlooked species. More accurate classification could also help researchers and land managers understand and manage effects on forestry and agriculture.
